job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Drafting Review: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Enforcement Gaps

Items are in section order. The most urgent ones are summarized at the end.

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** The threshold is per vessel, so an operator can split recovery across several vessels, each under 10,000 tons, and escape the ban entirely. It also leaves out recovery by anything that isn't a "vessel," such as fixed platforms, riser systems connected to installations, or autonomous seabed collectors operating apart from a surface ship.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), 10,000-ton threshold.** Everything below 10,000 tons per year is lawful. That likely covers pilot and test mining, which can damage large areas of seabed. The section also doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry (nodules come up waterlogged), or whether "per year" means a calendar year or any rolling 12-month period, which invites gaming and litigation.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery."** The trigger is *recovering* material, not disturbing the seabed. Collector trials that churn up sediment and create plumes, but discard or leave most of the material, may not count at all.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "seabed," "mineral resources," and "200 meters."** None of these is defined, and the bill doesn't say how depth is measured. "Mineral resources" could be read to include offshore oil and gas, which are treated as minerals under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. That could pull in deepwater drilling, generating industry opposition and a vagueness or overbreadth challenge. Or it could be read narrowly in ways we don't intend.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** "Secretary" is never defined anywhere in the bill. An agency could simply decline to act on that basis, and the provision is easy to attack in court.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), Secretarial determination.** Letting an official expand the scope of a *criminal* prohibition by "determination" raises nondelegation and fair-notice/vagueness problems, which makes (B) the likeliest provision to be struck. The bill also gives no standard, procedure, or rulemaking authority, and a hostile administration can simply never make a determination.

7. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition covers only citizens and corporations. That leaves out LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other entities (many mining ventures are LLCs) as well as lawful permanent residents. It also covers only entities "organized under the laws of a State," which arguably excludes entities organized in D.C. or the territories unless "State" is defined.

8. **Sec. 2(2) and Sec. 3(a), foreign subsidiaries.** A U.S. company can mine through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary or a foreign-flagged vessel, and neither is a "U.S. person." The bill has no ownership-or-control test and doesn't cover U.S.-flagged vessels as such.

9. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000-gross-ton floor means smaller vessels never register, even though they can still recover minerals. "Equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources" is vague: operators can argue that removable or leased equipment doesn't make a vessel "equipped."

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

10. **Sec. 3(a), "in the United States."** "United States" isn't defined. A foreign company operating on the U.S. continental shelf or in the EEZ may not be a "person in the United States," so the bill may not even reach mining in U.S. waters by foreign firms. The definition should expressly include the territorial sea, EEZ, and continental shelf, including those of the territories.

11. **Sec. 3(a), activities not covered.** Only *engaging in* mining is prohibited. Financing, insuring, sponsoring, chartering vessels to, buying from, processing, or importing minerals from deep-sea mining all remain legal, so U.S. capital and markets can keep the industry going offshore. "Engage in" is also ambiguous for parties who charter or contract out the actual work.

12. **Sec. 3(b), grandfather clause (major).** This exempts *mining*, not just exploration, conducted under any pre-enactment "exploration license." It has no time limit, no tonnage cap, and no rule on renewals, transfers, or amendments, so existing license holders could go to commercial-scale recovery indefinitely.
    - "Exploration license" isn't limited to licenses issued by NOAA under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA). It could be read to include ISA exploration contracts or foreign licenses.
    - The heading says "Existing Operations," but the text covers licenses, whether or not any operations exist.

13. **Sec. 3(b) and Sec. 8, rush-to-license window.** Because the exemption keys to licenses issued before *enactment*, companies have an incentive to obtain licenses during the pendency of the bill. Nothing stops an agency from issuing them in that period.

14. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment (major).** "Activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment" is undefined, unlimited in scale, and requires no permit, approval, or oversight. Any operator can say its recovery is "assessment," and full-scale test mining could be described this way. This exemption could swallow the rule.

15. **Sec. 3 generally, existing law.** The bill doesn't repeal, amend, or override DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) or OCSLA's hard-mineral leasing authority. Agencies would keep statutory authority to issue licenses, permits, and leases for the very activity being banned. That creates a conflict that courts and agencies will have to resolve, possibly not in our favor.

## Sec. 4: Registry

16. **Sec. 4, unenforceable.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of *Sec. 3*. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false report carries no penalty under this Act; 18 U.S.C. 1001 might reach false statements, but that is uncertain and not designed for this.

17. **Sec. 4(b), report contents and verification.** Reports only have to "describe" recovery activities. Nothing requires tonnage (the very figure the ban depends on), location, depth, or affiliated vessels, and nothing provides for verification, inspection, observers, or vessel tracking. Self-certification can't detect vessel-splitting or threshold evasion.

18. **Sec. 4, scope.** The bill doesn't say whose vessels must register (U.S.-flagged? any vessel worldwide? vessels in U.S. waters?), and it gives NOAA no rulemaking authority. Reports also aren't made public.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

19. **Sec. 5(a), per-day penalty vs. annual threshold.** The violation turns on an *annual* tonnage figure, yet penalties accrue "for each day." It's unclear when a violation begins (on day one, or only once 10,000 tons is crossed?). That invites challenges to any penalty calculation.

20. **Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 8, conflicting dates.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. The text is internally inconsistent about whether conduct in that window is penalized, and defendants will exploit the ambiguity.

21. **Sec. 5, no enforcing agency or tools.** The bill doesn't say who assesses civil penalties or by what procedure. It provides no authority to board, inspect, or subpoena, and no forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or recovered minerals. Without forfeiture, a fine can become a cost of doing business.

22. **Sec. 5, no injunctions or citizen suits.** There is no provision for injunctive relief to stop ongoing mining and no citizen-suit provision. Enforcement depends entirely on the executive branch's willingness to act.

23. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully."** Willfulness generally requires proof that the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful, which is hard to prove. Combined with the vague definitions above, defendants can plausibly claim they believed they were under the threshold or exempt.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

24. **Sec. 6, "seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months."** It's ambiguous whether 18 months is the deadline to *begin* or to *conclude* negotiations. "Seek to" is satisfied by minimal effort, and there is no reporting requirement or consequence. In practice this is hortatory.

25. **Sec. 6, "equivalent to those in section 3."** This would export the bill's own loopholes (the threshold, the vessel-splitting gap, the exemptions) into the treaty template.

## Sec. 7: Duration

26. **Sec. 7(b), 10-year sunset (major).** The whole Act expires after 10 years, regardless of the science or of whether Congress ever acts under Sec. 7(a). This directly contradicts 7(a)'s "until Congress finds" structure and turns a prohibition into a 10-year moratorium. It is the single biggest gap relative to our goal of a lasting ban.

27. **Sec. 7(a), lifting mechanism.**
    - "Serious harm" is undefined and is a lower bar than our "irreversible damage" concern.
    - Nothing requires the National Academies report to be commissioned, funded, or completed.
    - Because a joint resolution is just ordinary legislation, 7(a) adds little protection; any future Congress could repeal the Act anyway.

## Sec. 8: Effective Date

28. **Sec. 8, 180-day delay.** Companies get six months of lawful operation after enactment to ramp up, stockpile, or restructure (for example, into foreign subsidiaries or multi-vessel arrangements). This is combined with the date conflicts noted in items 13 and 20.

## Missing Provisions

29. **No severability clause.** Given the vulnerability of Sec. 2(1)(B), the bill should state expressly that invalidating one provision leaves the rest intact.

30. **No rulemaking authority, designated lead agency, or authorization of appropriations.** Without these, NOAA and other agencies may lack the mandate or resources to implement the registry and enforcement.

## Highest Priority for the Markup

If you can push only a few amendments, focus on these:

- **#26:** the 10-year sunset.
- **#12 and #14:** the grandfather and environmental-assessment exemptions.
- **#1 and #2:** the per-vessel threshold.
- **#8 and #10:** foreign subsidiaries and the undefined "United States."
- **#11:** no ban on financing or imports.
- **#15:** no repeal of DSHMRA licensing.
- **#16:** the registry has no teeth.

I'm happy to draft amendment language or a one-page summary for Hill offices on any of these.
